issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the other two memory items, which describe intrusive, sensory-dominated, repeatedly replaying trauma memories. That combination is not impossible, but with no other items indicating organized narrative access, the 'very easily' wording pulls in the opposite direction and is clinically inconsistent within this node.

issues.item: Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of mugging/robbery. 'Being around children' and 'Happy families' do not show a plausible thematic link to the reported trauma, and there are no accompanying threat or appraisal items to explain why these social/family cues would specifically trigger this patient's robbery-related PTSD.

issues.item: Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
issues.explanation: 'I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation mainly links triggers and memory with maladaptive strategies, but the actual triggers and memory content given are socially/family themed and intrusive-image based; deliberate conflict-seeking does not fit clearly with those items and looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, triggers centered on children and idealized families are hard to link clinically unless there is additional trauma meaning not represented elsewhere. The memory items describe perceptual re-experiencing of the robbery, but these triggers imply family/child themes that are absent from the rest of the profile, making the trigger set feel disconnected from the trauma type.

Within the Triggers node, 'children present' and 'happy families' suggest a loss/family-comparison theme, whereas 'being criticised or corrected' suggests interpersonal shame or sensitivity. These could coexist, but together they do not form a coherent trigger pattern tied to a robbery, especially given no threat or appraisal items supporting these meanings.

'Happy families' is a weakly plausible trigger for a mugging/robbery trauma and is hard to connect to the accompanying memory items, which are purely sensory/reliving-based and suggest trauma reminders tied more directly to the event. It does not fit well with the otherwise robbery-linked trigger pattern.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking conflict/create drama' is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation links triggers and memory to maladaptive strategies, but the selected triggers and memory items imply intrusive re-experiencing, for which suppression/avoidance is coherent; deliberate conflict-seeking appears clinically disconnected and unusually externalising relative to the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Kwame Mensah, a 58-year-old Ghanaian American hairdresser, came to treatment nearly a year after he was mugged closing his salon in the evening. He had stayed late finishing a client, swept up hair, counted the register, and stepped into the alley behind the shop with the day's cash in a small bag. A man emerged from the shadows, unsteady and sharp-faced, reeking of alcohol. When Kwame hesitated, trying to understand what was happening, the man snapped at him to hand it over and stepped closer in a way that felt suddenly erratic and dangerous. What remained with Kwame was less a coherent story than a set of stark, silent pictures: the glint of the man's eyes, the dark mouth of the alley, the bottle-sour smell on his breath, the accusatory force in his voice. He said he knew exactly what happened, but when his wife asked him to describe it afterward, he found himself unable to put it into words. Instead, the scene returned as if a film had started up inside him, playing the same images again and again.

In the weeks that followed, those fragments seemed to attach themselves to moments in daily life. The smell of alcohol on a client who came in after lunch could bring the alley back so vividly that for a second he was no longer in the salon. If someone on the sidewalk outside the front windows lingered too long, moved furtively, or watched the cash register, Kwame felt himself tighten and scan for danger. What surprised him was how strongly criticism also began to affect him. If a customer corrected him sharply about a haircut or complained that he had taken too much off, the tone of being confronted jolted something loose, and the old visual sequence flashed up before he could stop it. Because the memory came in pictures rather than words, sudden and repetitive, he could not talk himself through it; he just felt captured by it.

Kwame responded by trying to force the whole thing out of his mind. When an image started, he would clamp down on it and tell himself not to think about the robbery. He also found himself replaying his own mistakes, dwelling on what he had done wrong that night-why he had taken the alley, why he had paused, whether he should have seen the man sooner. The more those film-like memories intruded, the more he turned them over afterward in self-blaming loops, as if finding the exact point of failure might somehow protect him. At work he became more withdrawn. He shortened conversations with clients, left the reception area to his junior colleague when possible, and avoided people he did not know well, especially men who seemed watchful or unpredictable.

Over time these habits made his world narrower and his alarm quicker to rise. Avoiding people meant he spent more of the workday on edge when he had to engage, with less of the ordinary ease that had once anchored him in the salon. He watched customers for signs that they might turn aggressive or suspicious, and because he was trying so hard not to think about the robbery, small cues seemed to hit him even harder when they broke through. A whiff of whiskey from someone waiting for a trim, a tense exchange in the chair, a stranger pacing outside the shop-each could set off the familiar strip of images. Those images, in turn, sharpened the sense that danger was close by and made other people's behavior seem loaded and risky. By now, criticism from clients had become especially hard to bear: a simple correction about sideburns or beard length could feel less like routine feedback than the start of another threatening encounter, and afterward he would spend hours going over his own failings.

His marriage had been affected by this shrinking. His wife experienced him as distant and hard to reach, particularly because whenever she asked what was replaying in his mind he would go quiet and say he did not want to talk about it. He was still working, but the salon no longer felt like a place of easy familiarity. It felt exposed. He finally sought help after snapping at a regular customer who had mildly criticized a haircut while another man in the waiting area smelled strongly of liquor; Kwame was flooded with the old images and had to step into the back room to steady himself. What frightened him most was that he seemed to be training himself to see threat everywhere and losing the ease that had defined him for decades. What he hoped for, cautiously, was to be able to stand in his own shop again without feeling that the alley was about to open up behind him.
